title: Viola
summary: A computed viola, outside the real spread: mostly too dark, attacks far too quick, a noisy band near 395 Hz that is ours. E3 and Gb5 sound 11.1 and 11.7 cents sharp (finger at the equal-tempered station); C4 and Db4 have it moved to the note. Every note is a string with diameters read from photographs of a playing viola, bowed by a finite-width bow with hair compliance on the friction law measured on real rosin (Woodhouse and Galluzzo 2025), driving a computed shell body (Cassavetti Stradivari outline, 209 modes) and its air cavity at 144 kHz. On every page but C3 and Gb5 the bow force follows bow speed at the start of the stroke (our choice of player move); C4, Db4 and E3 also see the string's omitted bending modes at the bridge and the finger stop (a residual-flexibility record; nothing fitted); G3 and C3 have their after-length moved off the exact sixth by the cello's printed ratio, borrowed. D4's string carries a loss borrowed from a violin D string on a rigid monochord (Schoonderwaldt, Guettler and Askenfelt 2008, Q 480); the other strings carry none. D4 and Db4 also carry three point masses on the shell's rib (the end blocks, a boxwood tailpiece and a Flesch chinrest, 124.6 g, translational only). C3 and Db4 carry the shell's wood loss raised 3.25 times, because the body's mode near 395 Hz reads Q 75 against 15 to 27 printed; D4, G3 and Gb5 carry a printed damping law instead (Bissinger 2008, a violin's fit borrowed: 1.0 % at 400 Hz, falling as f^-0.45), which leaves that mode at Q 52; A4, E3 and C4 each lost grader rows with the 3.25 times loss and again with the law and keep their earlier render, and C3 and Db4 lost rows with the law and keep the 3.25 times loss.
physics_present: a computed viola shell body: the outline of the Cassavetti Stradivari viola (Library of Congress), f-holes from its caliper sheet, plate thicknesses from Johannsson's viola table, spruce top and maple back and ribs, a 6.5 mm mesh and all 209 modes its 15 Hz to 5 kHz window holds; the string drives it through bridge flexibility; a 3.24 L air cavity through a physical neck; dry room air; played at 144 kHz on every note
the friction law measured on real rosin (Woodhouse and Galluzzo 2025, eq. 13), on every page

strings with diameters measured on a playing viola (Percival 2013, Table 3.2, from photographs, about 10 %), tension and density from Guettler; the bending stiffness is derived from Percival's measured inharmonicity, because no source prints a viola string's stiffness

D4: the string's own loss, from a measurement on another string and carried to this one (DERIVED and BORROWED): loss factors eta_F = eta_B = 1/480 = 2.08e-3, so that every mode has a damping ratio of 1.04e-3, from Table VI of Schoonderwaldt, Guettler and Askenfelt (2008), the D string of a monochord with a rigid termination (decay time of the fundamental 0.521 s, Q1 480; the rigid termination makes the decay the string's own loss; the numbers are from the repository's hand transcription of the table); the viola's open D is the same note. Assumed: only the fundamental was measured, so the loss is constant in mode number; the paper prints Q1 and tau1, not a split between the friction and the bending terms, so the two are equal; the make and core of the viola's D string are unknown. Nothing was set by comparing with a recording. With it the grader scores D4 4 of 14 inside the real-vs-real ruler, as before, and 4 strict against 2; the note starts 442 ms after the bow, against 313 ms before and 604 ms in the recording

D4 and Db4: three translational point masses on the shell's rib, the lumped masses of parts the shell does not model (no lever arm and no rotary inertia, so they cannot show a part's own modes): the upper end block 15.732 g and the lower end block 14.159 g (Johannsson's viola table, Medium: 50 x 18 and 45 x 18 mm by the 38 mm rib height; the table gives no wood, so the shell's own spruce pack at 460 kg/m3 is an assumption), the tailpiece 15.4 g added to the lower block for 29.559 g (Maderas Barber's Hill model boxwood viola tailpiece, 130 mm, ref. 11219; the same maker lists 25 g in ebony and 20 g in French boxwood, so 15 to 25 g, and the one this viola wore is unknown), and a Flesch chinrest of 79.3 g (Luthier Vidal's Wolf KH-21 listing, the only weight found for it; a Goetz Flesch viola chinrest lists 67 g with screws at Thomann), 124.59 g in all. Where they sit is our choice, and no print places them: 138 rib nodes at the top end, 128 at the bottom end, and 32 on the flanks of the lower end block for the chinrest (a Flesch rest is centre-mounted over the tailpiece; a first version that put it off the centre line on the bass side was withdrawn and is on no page). Loaded response of the D string: the body's 395 Hz pole goes from one peak at 395.10 Hz, Q 75.3, effective mass 34.0 g to one peak at 390.76 Hz, Q 73.5, effective mass 41.3 g, still under the 56 to 117 g printed for a viola. On the grader D4 ties (4 of 14 inside the real-vs-real ruler, as before; strict 4 to 3, spectral flux leaving the strict ruler); the note is 0.4 dB louder, 2.3 and 6.1 dB louder over 1.0-1.6 and 2.4-3.5 kHz, its tenth harmonic rises 18.8 dB from 31.7 dB under the strongest, and the grader's gap grows on 13 of the 14 measures with a ruler, none by a ruler's width (the centroid gap shrinks); it plays as more physics with each mass sourced, not for a better count. Neck and fingerboard are not represented: a print gives the fingerboard's size (Johannsson: 305 mm long, 24.5 to 45 mm wide) but no neck width and no mass, and a rigid point mass cannot carry the board's own modes. Db4 carries the same masses at the same nodes (rendered on 11-06 on its bridge-row card: 3 of 14 inside the real-vs-real ruler against 2, strict 1 against 2; the one row that changes sides on the loose ruler, spectral flux, goes from 0.928 to 0.919 against a ruler edge of 0.925, and odd/even balance leaves the strict ruler, 1.80 to 2.82; the note is 0.5 dB louder, with +2.3, -1.9 and +4.7 dB over 1.0-1.6, 1.6-2.4 and 2.4-3.5 kHz; the grader's gap grows on 8 of the 14 measures with a ruler and shrinks on 6, none by a ruler's width; it plays by the count rule as more physics, and its loose rise is the one flux row crossing an edge by 0.005). C4 was rendered with them too and does not carry them: it fell from 5 to 4 of 14 on the loose ruler (the band envelope left its ruler, 8.25 to 10.90 against an edge of 8.68) and its cepstral envelope gap grew by more than its ruler's width (7.70 to 9.06, against a width of 1.10), with the note 1.9 dB quieter. E3, Gb5, A4, G3 and C3 were not rendered with them
a bow of finite width with hair compliance, and bridge and bow flexibility
the after-length (bridge to tailpiece) at one sixth of the speaking length; on G3 and C3 it is the sixth times 116/115, the cello's printed ratio, borrowed because no source prints a viola's

stopped notes (E3, C4, Db4, Gb5): a rigid finger on the fingerboard (Issanchou 2017), a 1e13 N/m stop and a 3.5 N press; at its equal-tempered station on E3 and Gb5, and on C4 and Db4 moved to the note by one correction of 14.5 cents, the sharpness measured on the same string's phrase renders, with the bow at 1/11 of the sounding length from the bridge

C4, Db4 and E3: the string's omitted bending modes in series with the bridge spring and the finger stop (the engine's `residual-flexibility exact-static-green`: the exact static Green's function of the same tension, bending stiffness and pinned span, minus the retained modes' static sum; nothing is fitted and no tension, length or pitch is changed). A string seen through N retained sines cannot form the kink at a point support, so the retained modes alone are an upper bound and stopped notes come out sharp by an error that falls as 1/N; the row lowers C4 by 1.0 c, Db4 by 4.0 c and E3 by 1.2 c. The three pages tie their predecessors on the grader (C4 5 of 14 inside the real-vs-real ruler, 3 strict, as before; Db4 2 of 14, 2 strict, as before; E3 11 of 14, 9 strict, as before; no row changes sides and none is worse by a ruler's width), so they play it as more physics, not for a better count. They were rendered with a build of origin 29f5b261f plus a one-line fs-lbm change (sha256 af5a271295458164), not the cap binary of the other pages; with the row left out that build reproduces the previous C4 and Db4 renders to within one 16-bit sample step and the E3 render of the card before the bow-start change byte for byte; E3's present card was not rendered on it without the row. Gb5 was rendered with the row too and lost rows (8 to 5 of 15 inside the ruler: the partial-frequency gap went from 0.06 to 15.7 c, inharmonicity B from 0.0057 to 0.60, the attack gap from 5.05 to 5.93), so it keeps the retained modes alone. E3's attack is named: on its card before the bow-start change the row left 11 of 14 but shortened the grader's attack time from 102 to 39 ms against 558 ms in the recording; with the bow force following the speed from rest it is 134 ms (99 ms without the row), still far under the recording's 558 ms. A4, D4, G3 and C3 were not rendered with it

on D4, A4, C4, Db4, E3 and G3 the bow force follows bow speed through the start of the stroke; it is our choice of player move, not a measured player's bow, and Schelleng's printed relation, that both bow-force limits for Helmholtz motion scale with the bow speed, is why a force that rises with the speed is the consistent start; the numbers are the cards' own and D4's: force 0 N at rest, then a 0.15 s ramp to the card's bow speed (0.15 m/s) and the card force, and the final force and the release are unchanged. E3 and G3 were rendered this way on 11-06 and tie the full-force pages (E3 11 of 14 inside the ruler, 9 strict against 8; G3 7 of 14, 6 strict, its attack time 158 to 202 ms against 592), so they play it for consistency, not for a better count. Gb5 was rendered this way too and lost rows (8 to 5 of 15: the partial frequencies fall apart, 0.06 to 18 c), so it keeps the full force from the start; C3 was not tried

C3 and Db4: the shell body's wood loss raised 3.25 times (FoggyHill's loss packs on the spruce top and the maple back and ribs), because the body's bridge-coupled mode near 395 Hz reads Q 75 on this body against 15 to 27 printed for a viola (Coffey 2016, self-published); on C3 it is what lets the grader read the shell render as the named note, and on Db4 it also lowers the third harmonic, which sits on the shell's second bridge-coupled mode near 834 Hz. A4, E3, Gb5 and C4 were rendered with it too: the line near 395 Hz fell on each, but each lost one to three grader rows, so A4, E3 and C4 keep their earlier render and Gb5 carries the printed damping law instead (below). C3 and Db4 were rendered with the printed damping law too (below): each lost grader rows with it, C3 from 5 to 4 of 14 inside the real-vs-real ruler (the harmonic pattern and the odd/even balance each worse by more than their rulers' widths) and Db4 from 2 to 1 (the odd/even balance from 1.89 to 9.83 dB, out of its ruler), so they keep the 3.25 times loss. A4, E3 and C4 were rendered with the law too and lost rows with it: A4 from 10 to 9 of 14 inside the ruler (the wavelet spectrum, out by 0.2 dB), E3 from 11 to 8 (the cepstral envelope, the centroid and the partial frequencies, the last from 0.27 to 5.50 c against a ruler top of 1.25) and C4 from 5 to 4 (the band envelope, out by 0.07 dB), so those three keep their earlier render, the wood loss alone

D4, G3 and Gb5: the shell body's modal damping set by a printed law in place of the wood's own loss (Bissinger 2008, total damping of free violins, band-averaged over 400-5000 Hz: 1.0 % at 400 Hz, falling as f^-0.45; a violin's fit borrowed for this viola, radiation included, no radiating skin on these pages, the connection losses outside the law, extrapolated below 400 Hz); the body's 395 Hz pole rings down with Q 52 on D4's clip (G3's own second harmonic rides on the pole, so the ring-down can't be read on G3's clip, and it was not read on Gb5's) against 15 to 27 printed for a viola, so it is under-damped there and no factor was tuned to change that. The earlier D4 and G3 renders raised the wood loss 3.25 times instead (Q 26 at the pole), a factor with no print above 1 kHz, and the earlier Gb5 render had the wood loss alone (Q 75 to 76 at the pole). Gb5 scores 8 of 15 inside the real-vs-real ruler with the law, as it did with the wood loss alone (7 with the 3.25 times loss), 7 strict either way, and no row changes sides: a tie, posted because the law is printed damping
physics_missing: the shell's modal mass at the bridge is light against print: the body's bridge-coupled mode near 395 Hz has an effective mass of 34 g, where a printed viola's peaks give 56 to 117 g (Maestre, Scavone and Smith 2013, Fig. 4, one McGill viola, Q read from the figure), and the engine has no card knob for it but point masses, which D4 and Db4 carry (the physics list: with 124.6 g of sourced masses the pole is one peak at 390.8 Hz, Q 73.5, effective mass 41.3 g, still under the print); raising the wood loss 3.25 times lowers that peak 9 dB and leaves it 12 to 15 dB over the print, and on D4, G3 and Gb5, where a printed damping law stands in for the wood loss, the same loaded response lowers it 3.1 dB and leaves it 18 to 21 dB over

the finger moved to the note on E3 and Gb5: they sound sharp of equal temperament (E3 +11.1 c with the bridge row, Gb5 +11.7 c, on the posted pages), where the recordings sit below it; on C4 and Db4 the one correction puts the grader's pitch at -2.8 c and +1.0 c (with the bridge row; the previous pages read -1.8 c and +5.0 c, the Db4 one printed as +4.8 c), against recordings at -1.4 c and -22.1 c; the same 14.5 c correction was rendered on E3 and Gb5 (Db4's value, not re-measured on their strings) and each page lost a loose grader row (E3 from 11 to 10 of 14, Gb5 from 8 to 7 of 15), because every harmonic moves about 1 % against the fixed body modes (E3's fifth harmonic left the shell's 834 Hz mode and the note fell 2.3 dB), so both pages keep the equal-tempered station and their pitch error

what drives a noisy band of lines around the shell's 400.8 Hz pole (strongest near 395 Hz, noise-driven and not a comb, the same place when the note changes) and a fixed line near 200 Hz on the viola pages: neither is explained

the tone and the start of the note: most notes are too dark (D4 centroid 594 Hz against 1210 Hz in the recording) and start far faster than the recordings (D4 attack 104 to 442 ms against 604 ms, the string loss above having moved the page's from 313 to 442 ms; C4 80 ms against 342 ms)

harmonics-to-noise as high as the recordings: ours is lower on the pages that state it (C4 16.8 dB against 30.0 dB, Db4 21.4 dB against 33.0 dB; the 23.5 dB printed here for Db4 was its value before the 3.25 times loss)

string loss and bending stiffness from a source: no loss is printed for these strings; D4 carries one borrowed from a violin D string on a rigid monochord (Schoonderwaldt, Guettler and Askenfelt 2008, Table VI: Q1 480, a damping ratio of 1.04e-3 on every mode, the constant in mode number and the equal friction and bending terms being assumptions), and the other pages carry none; the stiffness is derived

the 3.25 times wood loss (on C3 and Db4) has no print above 1 kHz: it is a factor set on the body's lowest strong pole (Q 75 on the wood alone against 15 to 27 printed) and applied at every frequency, where Bissinger's (2008) total damping of free violins falls with frequency, from 1.0 % at 400 Hz to about 0.4 % at 4 kHz, at or below the wood's own flat loss and 2 to 7 times below the factor. D4, G3 and Gb5 carry that print's law instead (a violin's fit borrowed for this viola, radiation included, extrapolated below 400 Hz), which leaves the 395 Hz pole at Q 52 (read on D4's clip), twice the printed range; C3 and Db4 were rendered with it and lost grader rows, so they keep the 3.25 times loss, and A4, E3 and C4 lost rows with it too, so they keep the wood loss alone. On the D4 clips the 3.25 times render's band levels sat 5.8, 5.5 and 6.5 dB below the wood-alone render over 1.0 to 1.6, 1.6 to 2.4 and 2.4 to 3.5 kHz, and the law render sits 2.1, 1.9 and 2.8 dB above it, and on the G3 clips the law render sits 0.6, 3.5 and 2.1 dB above the wood-alone render and 4.0, 12.1 and 13.0 dB above the 3.25 times render over the same bands, and on the Gb5 clips 0.8, 0.5 and 5.5 dB above the wood-alone render and 8.8, 6.0 and 13.8 dB above the 3.25 times render, so the pages that keep the 3.25 times loss are probably too dark there by about that much. With the law, the viola D4 page's lines at the 6th to 11th harmonic sit 6.8 dB below the violin D4 page's (13.1 dB with the 3.25 times loss, 10.4 dB on the wood alone); 2.2 dB of that is the string's bridge force (the viola string's after-length makes holes at the 6th and 12th harmonics) and the rest nothing here accounts for
